Corinn Tiffany∗,1, Wen Zhang∗,1, Eugene Bagdasarian1,2, Lillian Tsai1
1Google, 2University of Massachusetts Amherst
Abstract
Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from tak-
ing rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and
enforcing it on the agent’s tool calls. In multi-step tasks,
however, which actions are valid often depends on what the
agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a
policy engine for enforcingstatefulcontextual policies. A
Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using
a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, de-
ferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We
show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an uncon-
strained agent’s utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked,
Sapien’s policies rule out 93–95% of attacks on AgentDojo
and 62–85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists
on long-horizon tasks).
1 Introduction
AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to autonomously
plan and carry out natural-language tasks by calling exter-
nal tools [15, 17, 39]. Unlike traditional programs governed
by hard-coded control flow, agents rely on the LLM’s rea-
soning to interpret tool outputs and dynamically plan their
next steps, allowing them to tackle complex, long-horizon
tasks. Increasingly, developers aim forgeneral-purpose agents,
equipping AI models with a broad suite of tools to handle
open-ended tasks across domains on behalf of a user—for
example, managing online accounts, organizing meetings
and notes, or coordinating travel.
Yet delegating tool invocation to an LLM makes agents
inherently unreliable and prone torogue actions—tool calls
that diverge from the user’s intent. As trajectories span more
steps, agents are more likely to encounter untrusted content
that hijacks them via prompt injection [19, 64], or to spon-
taneously drift from their goal, misinterpret a tool output,
or improvise an unintended workaround [ 25]. In practice,
